projectTitle: Engineering E. coli to express prbA, a paraben-degrading esterase, as a pre-treatment for food waste recycling
tagline: If preservatives are designed to stop microbes, can we design microbes to stop preservatives?
summary: HKSSC (St. Stephen's College, Hong Kong) noticed a bottleneck nobody was talking about: Hong Kong's O-PARK organic resources recovery centre runs anaerobic digestion on food waste, but the chemical preservatives already in that waste inhibit the very microbes doing the digesting. They cloned prbA, a paraben esterase from Enterobacter cloacae that hydrolyses parabens to 4-hydroxybenzoic acid and needs no complex cofactors, into pET22b+ under a T7 promoter with a pelB signal peptide directing it to the periplasm, then characterised it with CFU-based MIC assays, a pNPA esterase assay and HPLC. They won Best New Basic Part at high school level largely on the strength of the prbA part family - including the previously unregistered native promoter and RBS, which they located in silico with BPROM and then built into a promoterless GFP reporter construct. The dry lab and statistics are the standout: structure-guided mutant design in HotSpot Wizard on an AlphaFold model, and a Michaelis-Menten kinetic analysis defended with two-way ANOVA, a Brown-Forsythe Levene variance check and Welch-Satterthwaite contrasts with Holm correction.
awards: Best New Basic Part winner (High School)
Nominee: Best Village Project (Agriculture / Food & Nutrition / Fashion & Cosmetics / Art & Design)

dry.frameworks: Three distinct computational strands. (1) Structure and protein engineering: the prbA structure was taken from AlphaFold and visualised in UCSF Chimera, which revealed a long flexible N-terminal tail consistent with the 31-residue signal peptide and justified the Cycle 2 switch to pelB periplasmic targeting. HotSpot Wizard 3.1 (Loschmidt Laboratories) was then used for a full structure-guided mutagenesis workflow: stability hotspots were ranked by B-factor and relative accessible surface area (ASA), buried residues filtered out, and three candidates triaged - A198 (50% ASA, highest flexibility) rejected because the Correlated Positions tab showed it needs a compensating mutation elsewhere; P329 rejected because only one amino acid occurs at that homologous position; N240 (34% ASA) selected, with Amino Acid Frequencies showing histidine as the commonest homolog residue and Mutational Landscape giving Asp/His/Ser an 88% probability of preserving function. They used the Design Library function with a minimal frequency threshold of 10% to generate degenerate codons for saturation mutagenesis at N240 and back-translated an E. coli K12-optimised mutant sequence. A second, separate hotspot run targeted catalytic efficiency rather than stability, prioritising A221 and A140 (mutability score 6, both in the catalytic pocket and substrate access tunnel) and designing an RCY degenerate codon library giving 50% Ala / 50% Thr with ~94% chance of seeing both variants in 5 colonies. (2) Molecular docking: methyl-paraben (PubChem CID 117065203) was docked across the whole prbA structure using HotSpot Wizard's docking module and visualised in Chimera to confirm N240 is not in the ligand-binding region - and they honestly flagged that histidine ionises near pH 6, so the mutation could backfire. Earlier docking with CB-Dock2 in PyMOL identified the catalytic serines. (3) Promoter prediction: BPROM was run on the 247 bp upstream region of prbA, predicting a sigma-70 promoter with an LDF score of 5.30 (threshold 0.20), a consensus -10 box TATAAT at position 163 (score 68), a near-consensus -35 box TTGAAA at 142 (score 23), 21 bp spacing and TSS at 178. (4) Enzyme kinetics: a Michaelis-Menten model fitted to pNPA assay data, plus a 35-page mathematical modelling report, with Monod kinetics recommended by Professor Patrick Lee for future digester-scale work.
dry.dataviz: The wiki carries a 35-page mathematical modelling PDF embedded inline for the kinetics section. More interesting is how they made the data defensible rather than merely pretty: initial velocity versus substrate concentration plotted for all four enzyme conditions (1 and 10 ug/mL porcine liver esterase control, 1 and 8 ug/mL recombinant prbA), Michaelis-Menten fits overlaid, and the statistical validation laid out as readable tables with the F statistics, degrees of freedom and p-values spelled out and each test explained in plain language for a non-statistician reader. Every chart in results is captioned with a complete alt text describing the plate layout or chromatogram, and both HPLC calibration chromatograms and time-course chromatograms (T0, T1, T2, T4) are shown rather than just a summary number.
dry.datascience: This is the most statistically disciplined high school dataset of the five teams reviewed. Because they could only measure enzyme input by total powder weight rather than molar concentration, they refused to report kcat/Km and instead defined a mass-normalised catalytic capacity metric Q = Vmax / (Cmass x Km), valid only in the low-substrate regime (S << Km), with units cancelling to L g-1 min-1. Recombinant prbA at 1 ug/mL scored Q = 9.518 L g-1 min-1 versus Q = 4.545 for commercial porcine liver esterase at the same mass concentration - a 2.09-fold advantage. They then proved the difference was not pipetting noise: a two-way ANOVA across 4 enzyme conditions x 7 non-zero substrate concentrations gave enzyme condition F(3,64) = 52.530, p = 3.01e-17; substrate F(6,64) = 92.111, p = 1.49e-29; interaction F(18,64) = 21.012, p = 3.15e-20. A Brown-Forsythe Levene test (median-based, chosen over mean-based Levene precisely because outliers drag the mean) returned p = 0.01898, rejecting equal variances - so rather than ignore it they switched to Welch-Satterthwaite contrasts with Holm correction for multiple comparisons, confirming significance at 0.25 mM (p = 0.03452), 0.20 mM (p = 0.04225) and 0.10 mM (p = 0.00408). Separately, they chose CFU plate counts over OD600 for MIC determination because OD600 is confounded by precipitation and dead cells, and built an OD600-to-CFU/mL standard curve for proper per-cell normalisation. MIC was bracketed empirically: 400-500 mg/L methyl-paraben for wild-type BL21(DE3), 1000-1500 mg/L for the Cycle 1 prbA-idt construct, and 500-600 mg/L for the Cycle 2 pelB construct - and they published the awkward finding that Cycle 2 was worse than Cycle 1, diagnosed it from faint SDS-PAGE bands as a protein-isolation methodology problem, and opened Cycle 3 with 6xHis-tag IMAC purification to fix it.
dry.software: Two released pieces of software, both genuinely built rather than mocked up. FoodSafe is a native iOS app in Swift (source at https://github.com/judeliucodex/Foodsave, initial scaffold AI-assisted then refined by the software team) with two features: a 60-second swipe-left/swipe-right food-sorting game (100 points per correct call plus combo bonuses, backed by a food library for post-game review) and an AI-assisted food safety checker that sends a photo to DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash's vision model and returns a danger-meter rating with the observations behind the judgement. They are explicit about the limits - a photograph cannot establish safety, pathogens can be invisible, and the meter is an AI estimate, not a measurement - and about distribution, noting it is on TestFlight for invited testers rather than the App Store. Microbe Wars is a browser-based 2D arena game written entirely in Python by the team and hosted at https://igem-game.vercel.app, where the player fights paraben enemies as prbA using weapons like an enzyme pipette, with campaign/endless/practice modes, four difficulty tiers and a levelling system. On the parts side they contributed BBa_26SZRXOY (prbA CDS), BBa_264E443U and BBa_26XQ4J7K (stop/start-codon-free variants), BBa_262HI0IB (native promoter + RBS, the Best New Basic Part), composite parts BBa_26SU8KOK (pelB + prbA) and BBa_26MSEOFB (native promoter/RBS + GFPuv), colony PCR and Gibson primers, and a curated 'PrbA's Family' part collection (UUID 9f037d92-78bb-470b-b139-c4ce28d4cc86).
techniques: structure-guided saturation mutagenesis site triage (ASA, B-factor, correlated positions, mutational landscape)
whole-surface molecular docking to rule out interference with the active site
in silico sigma-70 promoter prediction then promoter-trap GFP validation
CFU-based MIC rather than OD600, with an OD600-to-CFU standard curve
mass-normalised catalytic capacity metric (Q) when molar data is unavailable
variance-homogeneity diagnostics driving the choice of post-hoc test
publishing a negative/contradictory cycle result and diagnosing it

good.publicEngagement: Education ran under a framework they called LITTLE GEM (Gauge, Engage, Modify), reaching ages 3 to 101 across one kindergarten (Pods Kindergarten, Wan Chai), two primary schools (SSCPS and Shap Pat Heung Rural Committee Kung Yik She Primary School), a senior centre run by Suicide Prevention Services, their own school, and partner high school teams. Formats were built per audience rather than recycled: a DNA rainbow coin-toss game booth at a public carnival that engaged over 170 participants in three hours; a 'Find a Match' food-waste card game and DNA clay-modelling for 3-6 year olds; strawberry and banana DNA extraction for primary students; a Kahoot quiz; a live beta test of the FoodSafe app; and an original comic book, 'The Tragedy of Margaret in Food Waste', which they also staged as a drama skit with Margaret the frog as the lead. For the elderly they ran a physical food-waste card-matching game and clay craft. Internally, the HKSSC iGEM Club ran 8 after-school workshops over 7 months for ages 11-16 (4 lab, 3 IHP, 1 software) covering DNA, pipetting and serial dilution with P200 and P10 micropipettes across 28 participants, gel electrophoresis, and DNA keychain making, with Wayground quizzes for review - a deliberate pipeline for future team members. They measured learning rather than attendance: at SSCPS, 0% of 20 students knew what iGEM was and 10% knew synthetic biology before the workshop, versus 100% able to state iGEM's core goal and define synthetic biology afterwards, with 100% successfully extracting visible DNA; at KYS the post-presentation Kahoot returned 90% (18/20) accuracy. They also moved from one-off baseline surveys to paired pre/post questionnaires after realising the carnival survey only measured perception, not learning gain.
good.ihp: IHP ran on a six-step cycle of their own design, the iCycle (Identify, Initiate, Interact, Insight, Improve, and a sixth step, Inspire), with the deliberate twist that Improve feeds back into Interact so broad stakeholders can be revisited. Stakeholders were sorted into four functions - Information, Implementation, Safety & Technical, and iGEMer feedback - and they covered the whole disposal-to-treatment pipeline: public and restaurants (disposal), EPD (collection), O-PARK (treatment). The design changes are specific. CityU Professor Patrick Lee told them flatly that engineered microbes cannot legally be placed in collection bins in Hong Kong and must be used in a controlled environment with a kill switch, which reshaped their entire safety and implementation framing; he also said demonstrating paraben loss is stronger evidence than showing translation and told them to use both HPLC and the pNPA assay alongside Monod kinetics - which is exactly what the results page then does. HKU advised them they were over-engineering enzyme optimisation, that expressing the protein was enough to demonstrate the concept, that they should focus on the bacteria rather than the enzyme, and that instead of immediately adding a kill switch they should compare growth rates of wild-type versus transgenic E. coli and determine MIC by growing bacteria across paraben concentrations - which became the project's central experimental design. The Environmental Protection Department replied by institutional email with real operating data: food waste pH is 4-6 and varies with contents, impurities are removed and the waste slurried with process water, and the slurry stabilises in a buffer tank for 2-3 days before digestion. HKSSC acted on both constraints, testing their microbes under different pH conditions (which is also why pH stability became the target of the HotSpot Wizard work) and adding bin-contamination messaging to their education workshops. The HKUST Black Soldier Fly Bin team confirmed preservatives are a real but under-documented problem, endorsed pre-treatment in the bin before food reaches O-PARK, and pointed out HKSSC had not considered how to feed their E. coli - advising a layer of food replaced weekly. The KYS student survey revealed a misconception that catering, not households, produces most food waste, and that students knew about the problem but not the solutions, so the team added Smart Food Waste Bin content to the comic and to later activities. The elderly survey showed forgetting purchased food was a key driver of waste, which generated a planned 'food record' fridge-inventory reminder feature for the FoodSafe app.
good.realWorld: The intended deployment is a pre-treatment step dropped into infrastructure that already exists - the EPD's smart food-waste bins in public rental housing estates and the front end of O-PARK's anaerobic digestion line - rather than a new facility, and the team repeatedly checks the design against real operating constraints (pH 4-6, impurities, 2-3 day buffer-tank residence, and the legal bar on releasing GMOs into public bins). They frame the contribution as a reusable framework rather than a single product: parabens are one preservative class, and the enzymatic pre-treatment approach is pitched as adaptable to other persistent inhibitors and micropollutants. Impact is mapped to SDG 4 (target 4.7), SDG 7 (target 7.2, higher biomethane yield from more complete digestion), SDG 11, SDG 12 (targets 12.4 and 12.5) and SDG 13. There is no formal business model, revenue forecast or regulatory filing plan on the wiki, and FoodSafe deliberately stops short of public App Store release on cost and effort grounds - both stated plainly rather than overclaimed.

gemsTakeaway: The copyable thing here is statistical honesty as a competitive advantage: HKSSC could not measure molar enzyme concentration, so instead of quietly reporting an invalid kcat/Km they invented and justified a mass-normalised metric (Q) valid only below Km, then ran a two-way ANOVA, discovered unequal variances with a median-based Brown-Forsythe test, and switched to Welch-Satterthwaite contrasts with Holm correction rather than ignoring the violation. Pair that with their habit of publishing the cycle that went backwards (Cycle 2's MIC was worse than Cycle 1's) and diagnosing why - a high-school-plus centre will gain more credibility from that than from any extra experiment.
